title: Windows Container Health Monitoring
exclusions: Detects Critical, Error, and repeated Warning events recorded by the Windows Host Compute Service (HCS) in the collected Hyper-V-Compute Admin and Operational channels. It does not prove that a container, application, Docker/containerd daemon, Host Network Service, storage path, orchestrator, image pull, health probe, or business transaction is healthy; inventory running containers; calculate container CPU, memory, disk, or network consumption; identify an OOM kill or restart loop without corresponding collected evidence; or cover Linux containers, AKS/Kubernetes control-plane state, Service Fabric, Azure Monitor, application logs, ETW, Docker stdout/stderr, or diagnostic Analytic traces. The SPL intentionally makes no undocumented EventCode-to-lifecycle mapping and does not infer a container name from rendered text. Windows event levels 1/2/3 are Microsoft-defined severities, while the five-minute window, one-event Critical/Error trigger, three-Warning trigger, five-minute ingest delay, and severity labels are local policy choices, not Microsoft or Splunk defaults. Missing channels, fields, hosts, or events are source-health failures, not healthy container state. This UC performs no restart, stop, delete, isolation, image, network, trace, or remediation action and makes no compliance claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the approved Windows-container host inventory and isolation/runtime scope; effective XML WinEventLog inputs and add-on version; representative raw HCS Admin and Operational events from each qualified Windows build; the independent channel-freshness and malformed-field search; version-controlled `windows_hcs_severity_events` saved-search SPL, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and result rows; dashboard and alert-action revisions; exact event records exported from Event Viewer or `Get-WinEvent`; runtime/orchestrator and application-health correlation; bounded exceptions; responder disposition; and dated positive, negative, boundary, duplicate, delay, and missing-source tests. Each result should preserve endpoint, channel, provider, event ID, numeric level, event-record identity, count, first/last time, and policy branch. This documentation-only review created no Windows, container, HCS, Splunk, alert, dashboard, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index and fixed equivalent of the closed search window, ingest one XML event from `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, with `Computer=wc-host-01.example`, `Provider_Name=Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute`, integer `EventCode=999001`, `Level=2`, and `EventRecordID=101`; expect exactly one `error_or_critical` row with count 1 and all identities retained. Separately ingest three distinct Level 3 Operational events for the same endpoint/provider/EventCode in one five-minute bucket and expect one `repeated_warning` row with count 3. The synthetic event ID deliberately tests generic severity handling and asserts no undocumented lifecycle meaning.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero primary rows for each: one Level 3 Warning; two Level 3 Warnings; any number of Level 4 Informational or Level 5 Verbose events; events outside the exact two HCS sources; an HCS event missing endpoint, provider, integer event ID, numeric Level, or event-record identity; a Level value of 0, 6, or nonnumeric text; and events arriving only in the five-minute delay interval. Replay one identical event-record identity and verify deduplication prevents it from satisfying the three-Warning branch. The companion source-health search, not the primary alert, must identify missing expected hosts/channels, stale ingestion, malformed required fields, and duplicate routes.

dataSources: Primary sources are the Microsoft-documented Host Compute Service channels `Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin` and `Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Operational`, collected locally as XML with Splunk `[WinEventLog://<channel>]` inputs. Local conventions are `index=wineventlog`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, and `source=XmlWinEventLog:<channel>`. The SPL requires endpoint (`dest`, `Computer`, `ComputerName`, or `host`), provider (`Provider_Name` or compatible alias), integer `EventCode`, numeric Microsoft event `Level`, and `EventRecordID`/`RecordNumber`; `_raw` hash is a diagnostic fallback only. Docker Engine Application events, runtime inventory/events, HNS channels, orchestrator state, application telemetry, and Microsoft Log Monitor output are supporting sources and are not silently joined into this HCS detector.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) supplies Windows Event Log collection and XML/classic knowledge. Deploy approved input settings through a local deployment app; a local observability app owns saved search `windows_hcs_severity_events`, source-health search, dashboard, fixtures, exception lookup, and alert routing. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" (source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin" OR source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Operational") earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval endpoint=lower(coalesce(nullif(trim(dest),""),nullif(trim(Computer),""),nullif(trim(ComputerName),""),nullif(trim(host),""))), provider=coalesce(nullif(trim(Provider_Name),""),nullif(trim(ProviderName),""),nullif(trim(SourceName),"")), event_id=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID,event_id)), event_level=tonumber(Level), event_record_id=trim(tostring(coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber)))
| where len(endpoint)>0 AND len(provider)>0 AND isnotnull(event_id) AND event_id=floor(event_id) AND in(event_level,1,2,3) AND len(event_record_id)>0
| eval event_identity=endpoint."|".source."|".provider."|".event_record_id
| dedup event_identity
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as severity_events min(_time) as first_event_time max(_time) as last_event_time values(event_record_id) as event_record_ids by _time endpoint source provider event_id event_level
| eval signal=case(in(event_level,1,2),"error_or_critical",event_level=3 AND severity_events>=3,"repeated_warning")
| where isnotnull(signal)
| eval local_severity=case(event_level=1,"critical",event_level=2,"high",event_level=3,"medium"), first_event_time=strftime(first_event_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), last_event_time=strftime(last_event_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), warning_threshold=3, use_case="UC-1.2.95"
| table _time endpoint source provider event_id event_level signal local_severity severity_events warning_threshold event_record_ids first_event_time last_event_time use_case
| sort 0 -event_level -severity_events endpoint event_id
description: Detects Microsoft Host Compute Service Critical or Error events immediately and repeated same-ID Warnings in complete five-minute buckets from the Windows Hyper-V-Compute Admin and Operational channels. It preserves host, channel, provider, event ID, level, record identity, and count without assigning undocumented container lifecycle meanings to numeric event IDs.
value: HCS is part of the Windows container control path, so its severe events can provide early, host-level evidence when container creation or compute operations need investigation. A generic severity contract remains portable across qualified Windows builds, while strict source and record identity avoid presenting duplicate routes, informational lifecycle noise, missing telemetry, or guessed event semantics as a trustworthy container-health verdict.
implementation: Collect both Microsoft-documented HCS Admin and Operational channels as XML from every governed Windows container host, validate the actual provider and field shape on each supported build, and operate channel/source health independently. Save the SPL as `windows_hcs_severity_events`; run it five minutes after each closed five-minute event-time bucket. Trigger on any Level 1/2 result or three same-host/channel/provider/EventCode Level 3 records, then correlate with runtime inventory, Docker/containerd/Application logs, HNS, orchestrator, application health, and the raw HCS event before response. Treat all thresholds and severities as reviewed local policy.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows Containers — HCS Event Health`: show expected-host/channel freshness, malformed records, duplicate routes, and indexing delay first. Then show Critical/Error count, repeated-Warning count, affected hosts, and top provider/event IDs, with a table preserving source, numeric level, event ID, count, first/last UTC time, and record IDs. Add 24-hour and 30-day trends by host, channel, level, and event ID and drill down to raw XML, same-time Event Viewer/`Get-WinEvent`, runtime/orchestrator state, HNS, Docker/containerd/Application logs, and application health. Never label a host or container healthy merely because the panel is empty.
schema: Raw XML Windows Host Compute Service Admin and Operational events with Microsoft event-level semantics
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the primary alert. No CIM dataset is asserted to preserve the exact HCS channel, provider, event ID, numeric Windows level, event-record identity, and build-specific payload. The Performance model cannot establish HCS control-plane health, and generic CPU utilization cannot identify a container or an HCS failure. A purpose-built summary is acceptable only after raw-event parity tests preserve all identities, duplicates, delay, and source-health states.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row is a true match to the documented event-level and count policy, not proof that a container or application failed.

1. **Approved runtime, host, image, or container maintenance** — Starts, stops, upgrades, image cleanup, feature changes, and host reboot work can produce HCS warnings or errors while an operator is already managing the impact. Confirm exact change, host, runtime, event payload, start/end, owner, and successful post-change validation; an approved window does not make unexpected repeated errors harmless.

2. **Deliberate negative or resilience test** — A test may request an invalid image/isolation combination, stop a dependency, or exercise failure handling. Require a named test, isolated scope, approver, exact UTC interval, affected host, expected event ID/level, and rollback. Never break production HCS merely to test this search.

3. **Unsupported or incompatible host/image/runtime combination** — The alert can correctly expose a deployment mistake rather than an infrastructure outage. Compare host build, image tag, process versus Hyper-V isolation, runtime version, and Microsoft's compatibility guidance. Resolve the incompatibility; do not suppress the event fleetwide.

4. **Short-lived caller error with successful retry** — An orchestrator or runtime can issue a bad or racing operation and then recover. Check operation correlation, container/runtime state, retry count, user-visible health, and whether the same event repeats. Close only with positive runtime and application evidence.

5. **Duplicate ingestion route** — Direct collection plus Windows Event Forwarding, checkpoint replay, or restored logs can repeat one record. The SPL deduplicates exact host/channel/provider/record identity inside the window, but the source-health control must still report duplicate routes and preserve `_indextime` evidence.

6. **Provider/build payload change** — A Windows update can retain the level and event ID while changing payload or operational significance. Verify raw XML and Event Viewer text against the qualified build; do not pin remediation to message order or an undocumented ID dictionary.

7. **Warnings are expected at low frequency** — One or two warnings in a bucket intentionally do not page under the example policy. Trend them and review if they accumulate across buckets or correlate with restarts, failed probes, or user impact. The count threshold is a local noise-control choice, not a health guarantee.

**Safe notification suppression:** apply an exception only after the base result, keyed by exact `endpoint,source,provider,event_id` plus numeric inclusive `valid_from_epoch` and exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject wildcards, host-wide or provider-wide permanent exceptions, and suppression of source-health failures. Preserve matched findings in a review index and expire the entry automatically.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Windows Host Compute Service event monitoring; no adversary behavior or intent is asserted)
detectionType: Windows event severity with repeated-Warning persistence
hardware: Windows Server container hosts using process or Hyper-V isolation and exposing the Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute Admin and Operational channels. Container hosts managed only through a service-specific telemetry plane, non-Windows nodes, application-only containers, and environments without these channels require a separate source and identity contract.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft Windows container troubleshooting, HCS channel, event-level, and isolation-mode documentation plus Splunk Windows Event Log and Microsoft Windows add-on source-type documentation; channel availability, provider/payload fields, Windows/runtime/add-on/Splunk versions, thresholds, fixtures, source health, alerting, dashboard, and production response were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Splunk/container-platform/Windows-operations SME signed

cost.search_load_notes: The scheduled search reads two narrow HCS XML sources for one closed five-minute window, deduplicates by event-record identity, and aggregates by host/channel/provider/event ID/level. Actual ingest depends on container-host count and HCS warning volume; Analytic/debug traces are excluded.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and health boundary

Assign Windows-container platform, runtime/orchestrator, application, Splunk collection/content, and incident owners. Inventory every in-scope Windows container host, Windows build, runtime and version, isolation mode, orchestrator, service owner, and the two expected HCS channels. Microsoft documents process and Hyper-V isolation as different runtime boundaries and documents the Host Compute Service Admin and Operational channels as HCS troubleshooting sources. This UC watches those host control-plane events only. It is not a container inventory, resource monitor, readiness probe, application SLI, or proof that all expected telemetry arrived.

Install a currently supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows and qualify the exact add-on, Universal Forwarder, Windows, runtime, parsing tier, and Splunk versions in nonproduction. The forwarder service identity needs read access to the selected event channels and its existing outbound Splunk route; it does not need Docker/containerd administration, Hyper-V administration, container namespace access, image-registry credentials, service-control rights, or permission to stop workloads. Search and alert roles need read access to the event index and only the permissions required to schedule and deliver the result.

Use Microsoft's numeric event levels exactly: 1 Critical, 2 Error, 3 Warning, 4 Informational, and 5 Verbose. The primary detector accepts only 1-3. It pages once for a Critical or Error event and after three same-endpoint/channel/provider/event-ID Warnings inside one closed five-minute bucket. These count and timing choices are a deployment starting policy. Do not call them Windows defaults, map a numeric EventCode to create/start/stop without build-specific primary documentation, or infer a container identity by regex over localized message text.

## Step 1 — Collect both HCS channels as XML

On a representative host, verify the channel names with Event Viewer under **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows** and with:

```powershell
Get-WinEvent -ListLog Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin
Get-WinEvent -ListLog Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Operational
Get-WinEvent -LogName Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin -MaxEvents 20
Get-WinEvent -LogName Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Operational -MaxEvents 20
```

Deploy app-owned inputs rather than editing an add-on `default` directory:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin]
disabled = 0
index = wineventlog
renderXml = 1
current_only = 0

[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Operational]
disabled = 0
index = wineventlog
renderXml = 1
current_only = 0
```

Splunk documents `[WinEventLog://]` collection and XML rendering; current add-on documentation distinguishes XML channels with `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:<channel>`. Confirm the effective result with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`. Initial backlog collection can surface old events; the alert uses event-time windows, but source-health must still inspect `_indextime`, checkpoint resets, and duplicate direct/WEF routes.

For each qualified Windows build, compare raw XML and Splunk fields. Require exact source, source type, endpoint, provider, integer EventCode, numeric Level, EventRecordID, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Preserve ActivityID, operation identifiers, HRESULT/error text, container/compute-system identifiers, and payload fields when actually present, but do not make optional build-specific payload mandatory in the generic detector. Search numeric level and stable XML fields rather than localized rendered message wording.

Create an independent source-health search against a governed host/channel inventory. Report a missing expected host or channel, stale newest event/heartbeat, malformed level/event ID/record ID, future event time, excessive ingest delay, duplicate event-record identity, dual WEF/direct route, unexpected source type, provider change, and sudden payload/extraction drift. A quiet HCS channel can be normal; prove collection with configuration inventory or a safe approved canary, not by deliberately causing a production fault.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the SPL

Save the sidecar SPL verbatim as `windows_hcs_severity_events`. Schedule it every five minutes after the five-minute delay. At 12:15, `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` examines 12:05 through but not including 12:10, leaving five minutes for indexing. Measure p99 event delay and move both bounds together if needed so buckets remain closed and nonoverlapping.

The base search fixes the two XML HCS sources. `eval` normalizes endpoint and provider aliases and converts event ID and Level to numbers. `where` rejects incomplete identity, noninteger event IDs, unsupported levels, and missing record identity from trusted alerting; each rejection must remain visible in source health. `event_identity` joins endpoint, channel, provider, and record ID so a replay in one route does not inflate the count. Investigate duplicates rather than treating deduplication as collection repair.

After five-minute binning, `stats` counts one exact host/channel/provider/event-ID/level group and keeps its first/last event times and record IDs. Level 1 or 2 produces `error_or_critical` at count one. Level 3 produces `repeated_warning` only at count three or more. Equality at three alerts. A Level 4/5 record never enters the result, and a missing record does not become zero. Local severity is routing metadata, not the Windows event level or a business-impact verdict.

Do not append generic Perfmon rows. Host CPU can be high while HCS is healthy, and an HCS error can occur while host CPU is low. A generic performance data model also lacks stable container identity and cannot establish runtime or application health. Build separate source-backed UCs for runtime inventory/restarts, per-container resource telemetry, HNS/network failures, and application probes, then correlate after each detector preserves its own denominator.

## Step 3 — Validate semantics, boundaries, and collection

Use the exact isolated controls in `controlTest` with fixed event and dispatch times. A synthetic unused EventCode is intentional: the test proves severity handling without inventing event semantics. Assert exact source, provider, endpoint, level, integer event ID, record IDs, count, branch, UTC times, threshold, and use-case label. Test Level 1 and 2 separately at count one and Level 3 at counts two, exactly three, and four. Test Levels 4/5, malformed values, missing identities, a record at each time boundary, five-minute delayed arrival, duplicate replay, same record number on different hosts/channels, and different event IDs in one bucket.

On a nonproduction Windows container host, perform only approved ordinary operations such as starting and stopping a benign container, then compare the indexed stream with `Get-WinEvent` by channel and EventRecordID. Ordinary operations are field/coverage tests and might produce only informational events; do not claim they test the positive detector. For a real positive, use a documented safe lab failure supplied by the accountable platform team or replay sanitized raw XML. Do not corrupt HCS, stop dependencies, consume host capacity, deploy an incompatible production image, or enable verbose Analytic tracing merely to make an alert fire.

Microsoft describes HCS Analytic/debug logs and WPR tracing as troubleshooting mechanisms. Keep them disabled during normal collection unless support or a controlled investigation requires them; they can be high volume and their schemas are outside this SPL. Qualify Docker Engine Application logging, containerd/runtime logs, HNS channels, Log Monitor application output, orchestrator events, and health probes separately before correlation.

Measure event volume, ingest bytes, channel retention/overwrite, forwarder lag, search runtime, scheduled-search skips, and alert volume under deployment and failure peaks. Keep `status=draft` until accountable Windows-container and Splunk owners accept exact channels, fields, delay, thresholds, controls, source health, dashboard, delivery, exceptions, and runbook on every supported build/runtime combination.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage and evidence

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`, putting telemetry trust above findings. Alert text should say `Windows HCS severe event policy matched on <endpoint>` and include channel, provider, event ID, Microsoft numeric level, branch, count, first/last UTC time, record IDs, source-health state, host/runtime owner, and drilldowns. Do not name a container unless a validated payload or runtime correlation supplies an exact identifier.

Responder sequence:
1. Confirm the result came from an accepted source/type and complete identity, and check source freshness, delay, and duplicate-route status.
2. Open the raw XML and compare the same channel/EventRecordID in Event Viewer or `Get-WinEvent`; preserve the unlocalized event data and HRESULT/payload fields.
3. Identify the host build, runtime/version, isolation mode, orchestrator operation, compute-system/container identity when present, image, and recent change.
4. Check current runtime inventory/state, restart count, operation result, Docker/containerd or Application logs, HNS/network state, storage, host System/Application events, and orchestrator events.
5. Validate the affected application's readiness, liveness, transactions, dependencies, and user impact independently. HCS evidence alone does not prove application impact or recovery.
6. Follow the platform runbook for a source-supported remediation and preserve before/after evidence.

Never automatically restart HCS, Docker/containerd, a host, or a container; delete a container/image/network; change isolation; evict workloads; disable security; or collect diagnostic traces from this result alone. Such actions can broaden outage impact and destroy transient evidence. Recovery requires positive runtime and application evidence plus absence of the relevant recurring condition across a locally defined observation period; silence caused by a stopped forwarder or overwritten channel is not recovery.

Retain the saved-search revision, raw event, EventRecordID, same-time host/runtime evidence, source-health output, alert delivery, ticket, and disposition under local operational/privacy policy. Event payloads can contain image, command, path, network, or tenant identifiers; restrict dashboard and export accordingly. The catalogue retention estimate is advisory, not a legal requirement.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and tune safely

- **No HCS events:** verify the host is actually in scope, both channels exist, channel enabled state, local `Get-WinEvent`, effective input, forwarder service access, checkpoint, queues, index routing, source/type, time bounds, and search role. Empty results are unknown until coverage is proven.
- **Level is null:** inspect raw XML, `renderXml=1`, source type, add-on placement/version, props/transforms conflicts, and the actual `<System><Level>` element. Do not parse localized `Message` as the durable fix.
- **Provider or EventCode changes after patching:** compare raw XML and provider manifests on the exact build, update qualified fixtures and documentation, and preserve generic level semantics. Do not copy an event-ID meaning from an unrelated Windows build or web forum.
- **Repeated duplicate records:** compare endpoint/channel/provider/EventRecordID plus `_indextime`, WEF subscriptions, direct inputs, restored EVTX data, and checkpoint resets. Correct routing; do not broaden `dedup` across different hosts.
- **Warnings are noisy:** break down event ID, host role, build, operation, runtime, image, and change. Tune with a narrow expiring post-result exception or a reviewed event-specific policy only after primary documentation and fixtures; do not discard all Level 3 events at ingestion.
- **Critical/Error is benign:** preserve the event, verify operation success and application health, then document the exact expected scenario. A one-event trigger is intentionally sensitive and can be routed by host/service criticality.
- **Alert lacks container name:** expected when the event payload does not expose a validated identity. Correlate ActivityID/operation or runtime logs; never extract a guessed name from free text and present it as authoritative.
- **CIM/tstats returns nothing:** expected. This detector uses raw HCS event semantics, not Performance-model CPU rows.
- **Search goes quiet after upgrade:** inspect channel/provider/input and source-health changes before declaring improved health. A quiet panel can mean extraction drift or lost collection.
grandmaExplanation: We watch the Windows service that helps create and run containers. Severe or repeated warnings tell the platform team where to investigate, but we still check the container and its application separately before calling it unhealthy.
